SECTION 2
SCOPE OF SERVICES
A. Background Information
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the Anchorage 
Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; AO No. 2000-
65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and fire employees hired July 1, 1968, or later retroactively 
became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans including a surplus benefit plan, all of 
which were created for the purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain 
in the service of the Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through 
the establishment of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and
their beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and Plan
III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994, for new command police and fire, July 
17, 1994, for union firefighters and all new union police officers October 5, 1994.
A nine-member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has sole and 
exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt delivery
of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and administration 
of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the Board and 
Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the primary
responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into the 
APFRS Plans. The Retirement System is also subject to an annual independent audit
commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial valuation and audit are provided
to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Municipal Assembly.

6 
B. Work Statement
The primary role of the Investment Consultant is to provide objective, third-party advice
and counsel that will enable the Board to make well-informed and well-educated decisions
regarding the investment of the Retirement System assets. The Investment Consultant
shall acknowledge its responsibilities as a fiduciary. The Investment Consultant must be 
a registered investment advisor under the Investment Advisors Act of 1940.
All proposers must carefully read and review the sample contract attached in Exhibit 2. The 
successful proposer shall be required to enter into a contract with the Board of Trustees of 
Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System, which will be substantially similar to the 
sample contract. 
Contractual services for investment consulting will include, but not be limited, to the 
following: 
C. Scope of Services
1. Investment Policy, Objectives and Guidelines
Assist the Board in the development and periodic review of a policy statement that
properly reflects the Board’s tolerance for risk and that best helps the Board meet
its rate-of-return, funded status and administrative expense objectives.
• Review of Investment Policy Statement at least annually
• Ongoing monitoring and interim alerts regarding significant investment 
manager firm changes or market events
• Watch list designation and monitoring of underperforming investment 
managers
2. Asset Allocation Studies
Conduct an asset allocation study to determine whether the current asset allocation
falls within the Board’s investment objectives and guidelines. 
• Conduct an asset allocation analysis at least annually with consideration of 
actuarial assumptions, market conditions and efficient frontier analysis

investment managers utilizing appropriate databases and other resources.

Services

AGREEMENT FOR INVESTMENT CONSULTING 
AND ADVISORY SERVICES
THIS AGREEMENT entered into this _____ day of __________ between 
_________ (hereinafter called “Consultant”), and THE BOARD OF TRUSTEES OF THE 
ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM (hereinafter called 
“System” or “Board”).
WITNESSETH:
WHEREAS, the Consultant is in the business of providing investment consulting 
and advisory services; and
WHEREAS, the Board is vested with the authority and responsibility for the 
investment and administration of the assets of the System, and;
WHEREAS, the System is a public employee defined benefit retirement plan that 
was established pursuant to Chapter 3.85, Anchorage Municipal Code to pay certain 
retirement benefits to eligible members from funds contributed to the System for such 
purpose, and
WHEREAS, the System desires Consultant to provide investment performance

NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the premises and mutual promises herein 
contained, the parties agree as follows: 
A. SERVICES OF CONSULTANT
Consultant shall provide the following services to System as shown below:
1. Investment Policy/Guidelines Development.
2. Investment Policy/Guidelines Review.

3. Asset Allocation Consulting.
4. Measurement by Objective Performance Analysis with quarterly 
written reports and oral presentations at a Board meeting on a quarterly 
basis, including:
(a) A review and analysis of rates of return, including 
stocks, bonds and all other types of investments in a 
summary review of the investment performance of the 
Plan’s portfolio. Such reports are to be delivered on a

and ending balance of each investment advisor’s

of common stocks, long-term fixed income, 
convertible securities, alternative investments, real 
assets, and short-term investments.
(c) A continuing overview of the current investment 
environment, with comments on the present investment 
strategy and recent performance.
5. Monitor and report on investment managers’ compliance with the

 documents and investment policy on a quarterly basis.

The System agrees to provide or cause its accountants, trustees, investment managers 
and legal advisors to provide information regarding income, investment performance, and 
other pertinent matters relating to the System as requested by the Consultant from time to 
time. The System, through its Director, also agrees to communicate the System’s cash flow 
needs and investment goals to the Consultant and to keep the Consultant informed of changes 
in System’s financial or actuarial situation, needs and goals. The Consultant shall not be 
required to verify any information obtained from the System or its accountants, actuaries, 
trustees, and legal advisors and is expressly authorized to rely thereon. The Consultant shall 
verify all information obtained from investment managers. 
C. CONFIDENTIALITY
 Except as otherwise provided by law, the Consultant shall retain as strictly confidential 
any and all information about System, the Board, the assets of the System, and investments 
or financial transactions regarding the System received in connection with performing any 
services contemplated by this Agreement, including, but not limited to, investment manager 
reports, financial statements, internal memoranda, reports finances or other business 
information disclosed by the System, the System’s custodian, or any investment manager, 
either directly or indirectly, in writing or orally (collectively “Confidential Information”). 
The Consultant will not, during or subsequent to the term of this Agreement, use the System’s 
Confidential Information for any purpose whatsoever other than the performance of the

services on behalf of the System or disclose the System’s Confidential Information to any 
third party, unless the System consents in writing to such use or divulgence or disclosure is 
required by law. It is understood and agreed that said Confidential information shall remain 
the sole property of the System. In the event Consultant receives a request or demand from 
a third party for the disclosure of Confidential Information, the Consultant shall promptly 
provide written notice to System of such request or demand, including a copy of any written 
document of such request or demand, within five (5) business days after receipt of such 
request or demand. The Consultant further agrees to take all reasonable precautions to 
prevent any unauthorized disclosure of such Confidential Information.
D. BASIS OF ADVICE
System acknowledges that the Consultant monitors and obtains information from a 
wide variety of publicly available sources and certain private sources. The advice provided 
by Consultant to the System is based on its analysis of such public and proprietary
information.

Consultant hereby represents that:
1. Consultant is not the System’s investment manager nor is Consultant 
in any way compensated by nor does Consultant have any affiliation 
with any System investment manager; 
2. Consultant will make all calculations according to the Global 
Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) method of calculating time 
weighted rates of return;
3. Consultant certifies that it is professionally qualified independent 
consultant eligible to evaluate the performance of investment

managers investing the assets of System;
4. Consultant is an investment advisor registered with the Securities and 
Exchange Commission under the Investment Advisors Act of 1940. 
Consultant agrees to promptly notify client of any changes in 
Consultant’s registration status.
5. Professional liability insurance shall be maintained by Consultant 
during the life of this Agreement, with a minimum coverage of 
$5,000,000. Consultant shall provide System with proof of insurance 
prior to execution of this Agreement and annually thereafter during

6. Consultant maintains a robust program of cyber-security to safeguard 
the account information of the System.
F. FEES TO CONSULTANT
In consideration of the services rendered by Consultant, the System shall pay fees in 
accordance with Appendix A to this Agreement. Consultant shall not accept or receive, 
directly or indirectly, any commissions, fees, or any other form of remuneration or benefit of

person or entity in connection with or relating to the System’s assets, any investment made 
by the System, or any services performed under this Agreement.

1. This Agreement shall be applicable only to the services individually prepared 
for System. It shall not relate to any advice given by any person or persons 
not specifically designated by Consultant in writing to perform such services.

By execution of this agreement, the Consultant acknowledges that it is a 
fiduciary of the System within the meaning of the Alaska Uniform Prudent 
Investor Act, A.S. 13.36.225, et. seq. Consultant recognizes that its primary 
obligation under this Agreement is to the System and that it will place the 
interest of the System above all others and will not enter into any agreement 
or take any action contrary to that obligation. 
2. Neither party hereto may assign, convey, or otherwise transfer any of its 
rights, obligations, or interest herein without the prior express written consent 
of the other party.
3. This Agreement represents the complete agreement of the parties with regard 
to the subject matter and supersedes any prior understanding or agreement, 
oral or written.
4. This Agreement may be amended or revised only by an instrument in writing 
signed by both parties.
5. System acknowledges receipt of Consultant’s ADV, Part II, an updated 
version of which shall be provided to System annually.
6. The validity of this Agreement and any of its terms, provisions, rights and 
duties of the parties hereunder, shall be governed by the laws of the State of 
Alaska. 
7. This Agreement may be executed in several counterparts, each of which shall 
be deemed an original.
8. This Agreement shall become effective upon execution.
9. Any action under this Agreement shall be brought in Superior Court of the 
Third Judicial District in Anchorage, Alaska or the United States District

Court for the District of Alaska. Venue for resolution of any dispute under 
the terms of this Agreement shall be in Anchorage, Alaska. In any action 
arising out of the enforcement or interpretation of this Agreement, the 
prevailing party shall be entitled to recover its costs and attorneys’ fees.
10. Consultant agrees to disclose, in writing, to the System, within seven (7) 
business days, if Consultant becomes the subject of an investigation by the 
Securities and Exchange Commission for alleged breach of federal securities

Statement of Investment Policy

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment 
performance history.
F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

10
but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are 
prohibited which provisions are adopted for use in 
this System.
(2) No transactions shall be made which might 
threaten the tax exempt status of the system.
(3) No letter stocks shall be purchased.
(4) No funds shall be borrowed.
(5) No short sales shall be made.
(6) No tax-exempt bond shall be purchased or retained
unless, on a comparable quality and duration basis, it
provides an expected return superior to that of a 
taxable bond.
(7) No private placements shall be purchased. 
However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

E. Minimum Manager Requirements:
In order to be considered as a manager for the system a firm must meet the 
following minimum standards:
1. The firm must have at least $500 million under management;
2. The firm’s portfolio must have a 5-year investment 
performance history.
F. Manager Guidelines:
1. Managers shall have full discretionary authority in the selection 
and retention of investments, subject to the provision of law, trust 
agreements, this Statement of Investment Policy as amended from 
time to time and investment management agreement between the 
System and the manager.
2. The responsibility for security selection shall lie with the managers.
The managers, however, shall operate within these investment 
guidelines which shall conform to applicable governmental 
regulations, and shall cover four specific areas: (a) diversification; 
(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.
a. Diversification:
(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the 
security’s weight in the agreed upon market index 
plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be 
requested as provided below in section (d).
(2) No security shall be bought unless it is traded on
one of the major security exchanges or the Over-The-Counter (OTC) market. Listed American
Depository Receipts (ADR’s) shall be an approved
investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a 
manager’s portfolio. The manager is required to provide
the Board with a list and explanation of the types of
derivatives they expect to invest in, the purposes for
holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a 
description of the risks associated with these 
investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

10
but individual issues must have a Flow Uncertainty
Index (“FLUX”) score of 15 or less.
b. Credit quality:
(1) Commercial paper must be rated P-1 and/or A-1 by
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s respectively.
(2) The total bond portfolio will maintain a minimum 
average credit rating of “BBB+” as rated by both 
Moody’s and Standard & Poor’s. For Purposes of
compliance with this Policy, the manager will 
adhere to the same ratings scale and policy as that 
employed by Bloomberg in the structure of the 
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index (utilizing ratings by 
Moody’s, S & P and Fitch).
c. Portfolio Duration:
Total portfolio weighted average duration should not
exceed 120% of the bond market’s duration utilizing the
Bloomberg US Aggregate Index.
d. Restricted transactions:
(1) Conflict of interest and transactions between a
fiduciary and parties in interest, as described in
Sections 406 and 408 of Title I, Employee 
Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), are 
prohibited which provisions are adopted for use in 
this System.
(2) No transactions shall be made which might 
threaten the tax exempt status of the system.
(3) No letter stocks shall be purchased.
(4) No funds shall be borrowed.
(5) No short sales shall be made.
(6) No tax-exempt bond shall be purchased or retained
unless, on a comparable quality and duration basis, it
provides an expected return superior to that of a 
taxable bond.
(7) No private placements shall be purchased. 
However, Rule 144A securities with registration 
rights are permitted investments.
(8) No non-exchange-listed derivatives shall be
purchased or sold by any of the System’s managers.

11
e. Exceptions to Manager Guidelines:
(9) The Board acknowledges that when it is in the best
interests of the System to invest in a collective 
vehicle (i.e. comingled fund or mutual fund); it is 
not possible to dictate specific investment 
prohibitions. Therefore, it shall be the duty of the 
manager of such commingled fund to report to the 
Board on a periodic basis, the extent to which the 
investment strategies differ from the Board’s SIP.
Periodically, the Board will review the differences 
and determine if the commingled fund remains in 
the best interest of the System.
(10) The managers may request exceptions to the
restrictions outlined in V.F.2. by written
request to the Board.
(11) All exceptions will be submitted in writing to the
Board who will, after reviewing and receiving 
advice from the Fund’s Investment Consultant,
render a decision with regard to the request at the
next board meeting.
3. Brokerage Transactions
The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023.

PART 1 -- Introduction and Goal of the RFP
1.1 INTRODUCTION - General Information
The Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund (IMRF) is requesting proposals from 
investment management firms to provide domestic equity small cap growth
investment management services. There is no expressed or implied obligation for 
the IMRF to reimburse responding firms for any expenses incurred in preparing 
proposals in response to this request.
IMRF reserves the right to reject any or all proposals submitted. All proposals 
submitted will be evaluated by members of the IMRF Investment Department staff
(“staff”) and IMRF’s investment consultant (“consultant”). Firms may be asked to 
make formal presentations of their proposals to the IMRF Investment Committee 
and/or the IMRF Board of Trustees (“Board”). Selection of the investment 
manager(s) is subject to final approval by the IMRF Board.
1.2 GOAL
IMRF is soliciting qualified firms to provide domestic equity small cap growth
investment management services. The intent of the contractual relationship will 
be to establish an ongoing relationship between IMRF and the selected firm(s) for 
the purpose of providing IMRF with investment management services.
1.3 QUIET PERIOD
The Quiet Period is the period of time beginning when the investment management
RFP is issued and ends when the investment management firm(s) is(are) selected by 
the Board or the process is declared to be complete.
Respondents shall not contact IMRF Board members during the Quiet Period and 
should direct all questions and communications to the Director of Investments,

Investment Department Manager, Executive Director or other contacts identified in 
this RFP. 
Incumbent investment management firm respondents may communicate with IMRF 
Board members during the Quiet Period, but may not discuss the investment 
management search with the IMRF Board members during the Quiet Period. The 
purpose of the Quiet Period is to ensure that all prospective investment manager(s)
have equal access to information regarding the search objective and requirements; 
to be certain that communications are consistent and accurate; and to make the 
search process and selection process efficient, diligent and fair.
The Quiet Period will be posted to the IMRF website to prevent inadvertent 
violations by investment managers responding to the RFP.
IMRF Board members and members of the staff not directly involved in the 
investment manager(s) search shall refrain from communicating with the 
respondents regarding any product or service related to the search during the Quiet 
Period unless this communication takes place during a formal site visit or interview 
conducted as part of the investment management search.
An RFP respondent will be disqualified for violating the Quiet Period.
Offering or providing anything of value to the IMRF Board members and members of 
the staff is prohibited.

PART 3-– Services to be performed
The IMRF continually seeks to employ investment managers who possess superior 
capabilities in the management of the assets for public retirement funds. The 
IMRF further requires those investment managers selected and working in its 
behalf to meet the following set of conditions:
A. To recommend actions which in their best professional judgment are in the 
best interests of the IMRF to meet the investment objectives. Such 
recommendations include but are not limited to: (A) the allocation of funds 
among alternative types of investments; (B) specific investment opportunities 
regarding the acquisition, retention or disposition of investments; and (C) the 
addition, deletion or modification of authorized investments.
B. To select brokerage firms that are to act as a securities broker with respect 
to the purchase and sale of assets of the Master Trust allocated to the IMRF. The 
investment manager or any entity controlled by or controlling it, or affiliate with 
it, shall not act as a securities broker with respect to purchases and sales of assets 
allocated to the Fund unless IMRF specifically approves such action. Subject at all 
times to compliance with its fiduciary obligations, the investment manager shall 
select such firm or firms in accordance with IMRF’s policy on goals for the 
utilization of minority broker-dealers as set fort in the Investment Policy. Our 
current minority brokerage utilization goal reads as follows:
“It shall be the goal of the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund that 
not less than 20% of brokerage from actively managed separate 
account portfolios be executed by minority, women business 
enterprise and disabled broker/dealers. Managers of high yield 
bond portfolios, small-cap international portfolios, micro-cap 
equity portfolios and emerging market portfolios are directed to 
use their best efforts to execute their brokerage through minority 
and women business enterprise and disabled broker/dealers. This 
goal will be reviewed annually.”

C. In the selection of broker-dealers with whom to place orders for the 
purchase or sale of securities for the IMRF, the primary objective of the 
investment manager shall be to obtain the most favorable results. The investment 
manager’s selection of a broker-dealer may take into account such relevant 
factors as (1) price and/or commission; (2) the broker-dealer’s facilities, reliability 
and financial responsibility; (3) the ability of the broker-dealer to effect securities 
transactions, particularly with respect to such aspects as timing, order size, 
execution of orders and the ability to complete a transaction through clearance, 
settlement and delivery; and (4) the research and other services provided by such 
broker-dealer to the investment manager which are expected to enhance general 
portfolio management capabilities, notwithstanding the fact that the IMRF may not 
be the direct or exclusive beneficiary of such services. The investment manager’s 
selection of such broker-dealers shall be in accordance with Article I of the Illinois 
Pension Code (40 ILCS 5/1-101 et seq.), the federal Investment Advisors Act of 
1940 and any other applicable securities laws, rules and regulations.
D. To report to the IMRF in writing, monthly, on the composition and relative 
performance , both gross and net of fees, of the investments in their designated 
portfolios; the investment outlook for the near and long term; significant changes 
in the portfolio during the month; and the reasons for any significant differences 
between the performance of their portfolios and the appropriate market indices 
or other performance benchmarks established by the IMRF and the investment 
manager.
E. Additional responsibilities as detailed in each investment manager's 
agreement with the IMRF.

8.1 SELECTION PROCESS
Staff and consultant shall objectively review the proposal’s to identify qualified 
candidates based solely on the criteria presented in the RFP. Staff and consultant 
and members of the Board may interview all, some or none of the RFP 
respondents, undertake site visits to respondent offices and conduct such other 
due diligence as is prudent under the circumstances.
Staff and consultant will prepare a report and present the report to the 
Investment Committee during a public meeting of the Investment Committee.
The Investment Committee may interview finalists and will determine if a 
recommendation for the award of a contract will be made to the Board. The 
Board shall then act on the recommendation of the Investment Committee.
During the selection process all respondents to the RFP will be evaluated and 
ranked on four primary factors:
(a) People - stability of the organization, ownership structure and documented 
experience of key professionals
(b) Process - clearly defined, reasonable and repeatable investment strategy
(c) Performance - documented ability to meet investment performance 
benchmarks
(d) Pricing - fee schedule and associated costs
Staff and consultant are required to identify all minority and women-owned firms 
and firms owned by persons with a disability in the report presented to the 
Investment Committee. Staff and consultant must specify the reasons when these 
firms are not brought forward as finalists.
IMRF reserves the right to reject any respondents due to noncompliance with the 
requirements and instructions in the RFP.

PART 1 -- Introduction and Goal of the RFP
1.1 INTRODUCTION - General Information
The Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund (IMRF) is requesting proposals from 
investment management firms to provide domestic equity small cap growth
investment management services. There is no expressed or implied obligation for 
the IMRF to reimburse responding firms for any expenses incurred in preparing 
proposals in response to this request.
IMRF reserves the right to reject any or all proposals submitted. All proposals 
submitted will be evaluated by members of the IMRF Investment Department staff
(“staff”) and IMRF’s investment consultant (“consultant”). Firms may be asked to 
make formal presentations of their proposals to the IMRF Investment Committee 
and/or the IMRF Board of Trustees (“Board”). Selection of the investment 
manager(s) is subject to final approval by the IMRF Board.
1.2 GOAL
IMRF is soliciting qualified firms to provide domestic equity small cap growth
investment management services. The intent of the contractual relationship will 
be to establish an ongoing relationship between IMRF and the selected firm(s) for 
the purpose of providing IMRF with investment management services.
1.3 QUIET PERIOD
The Quiet Period is the period of time beginning when the investment management
RFP is issued and ends when the investment management firm(s) is(are) selected by 
the Board or the process is declared to be complete.
Respondents shall not contact IMRF Board members during the Quiet Period and 
should direct all questions and communications to the Director of Investments, 
IMRF Sample RFP

Investment Department Manager, Executive Director or other contacts identified in 
this RFP. 
Incumbent investment management firm respondents may communicate with IMRF 
Board members during the Quiet Period, but may not discuss the investment 
management search with the IMRF Board members during the Quiet Period. The 
purpose of the Quiet Period is to ensure that all prospective investment manager(s)
have equal access to information regarding the search objective and requirements; 
to be certain that communications are consistent and accurate; and to make the 
search process and selection process efficient, diligent and fair.
The Quiet Period will be posted to the IMRF website to prevent inadvertent 
violations by investment managers responding to the RFP.
IMRF Board members and members of the staff not directly involved in the 
investment manager(s) search shall refrain from communicating with the 
respondents regarding any product or service related to the search during the Quiet 
Period unless this communication takes place during a formal site visit or interview 
conducted as part of the investment management search.
An RFP respondent will be disqualified for violating the Quiet Period.
Offering or providing anything of value to the IMRF Board members and members of 
the staff is prohibited.
PART 2 -- Background Information on IMRF
2.1 PORTFOLIO DESCRIPTION
IMRF’s portfolio is a diversified and global portfolio having a total market value of 
$XX.X billion as of XXXX XX, 20XX. Approximately 99% of the portfolio is managed 
by outside investment managers. Approximately 1% of the total portfolio is 
managed internally by staff. IMRF strategic target allocations are as follows:

The IMRF continually seeks to employ investment managers who possess superior 
capabilities in the management of the assets for public retirement funds. The 
IMRF further requires those investment managers selected and working in its 
behalf to meet the following set of conditions:
A. To recommend actions which in their best professional judgment are in the 
best interests of the IMRF to meet the investment objectives. Such 
recommendations include but are not limited to: (A) the allocation of funds 
among alternative types of investments; (B) specific investment opportunities 
regarding the acquisition, retention or disposition of investments; and (C) the 
addition, deletion or modification of authorized investments.

to the purchase and sale of assets of the Master Trust allocated to the IMRF. The 
investment manager or any entity controlled by or controlling it, or affiliate with 
it, shall not act as a securities broker with respect to purchases and sales of assets 
allocated to the Fund unless IMRF specifically approves such action. Subject at all 
times to compliance with its fiduciary obligations, the investment manager shall 
select such firm or firms in accordance with IMRF’s policy on goals for the 
utilization of minority broker-dealers as set fort in the Investment Policy. Our 
current minority brokerage utilization goal reads as follows:
“It shall be the goal of the Illinois Municipal Retirement Fund that 
not less than 20% of brokerage from actively managed separate 
account portfolios be executed by minority, women business 
enterprise and disabled broker/dealers. Managers of high yield 
bond portfolios, small-cap international portfolios, micro-cap 
equity portfolios and emerging market portfolios are directed to 
use their best efforts to execute their brokerage through minority 
and women business enterprise and disabled broker/dealers. This 
goal will be reviewed annually.”
